claims.text: At high temperatures, high-entropy nanoalloy stability is governed by a balance between configurational entropy and elemental diffusional disparities.
Configurational entropy promotes homogeneous elemental mixing.
Differences in elemental migration or diffusion drive local segregation.
A sufficiently large entropy contribution can counteract differential migration and preserve a uniform solid solution.
If entropy does not counteract differential migration, local segregation and phase instability occur.
The nanoparticles initially have a statistically homogeneous random elemental distribution at room temperature.
Inert or reducing atmospheres avoid additional reactive driving forces such as oxidation.
Slow heating permits the nanoalloys to approach equilibrium at high temperature.
Surface and bulk atomic compositions reflect the degree of elemental segregation or retention of uniform mixing.
Configurational entropy at high temperature stabilizes a multielement alloy against phase separation by favoring random mixing.
Differences in individual atomic diffusion rates can promote local segregation despite configurational entropy.
Minimal atomic-size mismatch or small diffusivity differences favor entropy-dominated stabilization.
Under entropy-dominated conditions, the nanoalloy retains a uniform elemental distribution and structural integrity after high-temperature treatment.
An alloy engineered to have larger diffusivity disparities will exhibit more phase segregation or surface enrichment than the comparison alloy.
The prediction is limited to temperatures below melting or relevant phase-transformation points.
Oxidizing environments or extremely mismatched constituent properties may reduce the predictive applicability of the proposed mechanism.
